newsitem.title: USA: Japan economy to see more hard times -- U.S. experts.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy to see more hard times -- U.S. experts.

text.p: Faced with the prospect of more contraction in bank lending and higher taxes, Japan's troubled economy risks another year of anemic growth and further bank failures, U.S. experts said.
Japan's Economic Planning Agency predicted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of about 2.5 percent for the current year and 1.9 percent for the 1997/98 fiscal year which begins April 1.

Yet Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics, expressed serious doubts that Japan would achieve the EPA's forecasted growth rate, and warned that the economy might even contract. He said growth next fiscal year might come in "under one (percent) if they're lucky."

This week, the Nikkei 225 index sank more than 2000 points. With stocks under seige, analysts said, bank equity portfolios may shrink, making it harder for banks to meet international capital standards.
"What you're seeing is a catastrophic contraction of wealth," Weinberg said.
"With a reduction in wealth," he added, "you therefore have a reduction in the amount of credit the economy can support."
He emphasized that in Japan, more than in other countries, the economy historically has needed credit to grow.
To this end, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) has kept official rates at rock-bottom levels to bolster economic growth.
But as bank capital contracts and further constrains banks' ability to create credit, the BOJ's task could become tougher, analysts said.

"It means that the Bank of Japan has a very difficult job because it's maintaining a very easy monetary policy," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc. "It's pumping (liquidity) into the economy but that liquidity is not getting utilized in creating economic activity."
Ultimately, the liquidity will probably be used to purchase Japanese government bonds, causing market interest rates to fall further, Iggo said.
He said he also expects the liquidity to result in a weaker yen, and predicted the yen could depreciate to 125 per dollar.
On April 19, 1995, the Japanese currency hit a post World War II high of 79.75 per dollar. Since then, the yen has tumbled, trading at around 116 per dollar on Friday afternoon.
Analysts noted that any benefit to the Japanese economy from a further weakening of the yen is subject to a long lag.
In December, Japan's cabinet endorsed a final state budget plan for the coming fiscal year with an emphasis on cutting debt rather than nurturing economic recovery.
The budget also projected higher taxes, and some analysts warned this could put a further drag on growth.

"A number of tax changes will go into effect April 1 that will have a weakening effect on the economy," said Arthur Alexander, president, the Japan Economic Institute of America. "It's going to take spending power out of the economy."
While Alexander played down the risk of a financial system meltdown in Japan, he warned some banks could fail.
"I don't see a danger of system collapse, but there are dangers of individual organizations collapsing," he said.
Last year, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) ordered Hanwa Bank to halt its business, marking the first time in five decades the MOF had shut down a bank.
Analysts agreed that the Japanese economy is caught between a rock and a hard place.
Val Kosmider, head of international equity trading at Schroder Wertheim and Co Inc, warned that if the Nikkei breaks below the current 17,300, it might not stabilize until it hits 14,000.

Kosmider noted that Tokyo has shown it will not support the market and has tried to talk down the yen. The Japanese banking loan problems and other woes have to be dealt with. However, he added, "There can't be any hard steps, because who's going to fund it?"

Meanwhile, High Frequency's Weinberg said, "In fact, the only way Japan has out of this is ... to force lending even though bank capital standards and credit worthiness of borrowers may not be up to snuff."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1668 ))
